text: This is what in-house counsel actually sends back to a vendor: tracked changes and margin comments in Word. Producing a first pass takes one to three hours per contract.

Every company has a playbook — preferred, fallback, and walk-away positions. The bottleneck is applying it clause by clause across twenty to sixty pages, catching the term hidden in a definition three sections away, and doing it consistently with what the team accepted last time.

The naive approach is to paste the contract into a chat assistant. Our fair baseline is stronger than that: the same frontier model, the same playbook, the whole contract, one prompt. On short contracts it finds most issues — F one {{B1_F1}}. But only {{B1_CRR}} of its redlines meet every element of the playbook position, on forty-thousand-word documents its F one falls to {{B1_LONG_F1}}, and it cannot write into the document.
Playbook Redliner starts from the vendor's actual Word file and the company's versioned playbook: eighteen rules, each with a preferred, a fallback, and a walk-away position.
This is a real hosting and licence agreement from the evaluation set — an SEC filing with lawyer-labelled gold. We are Corio, the customer.
The document becomes a clause-addressable model. A planner maps every rule to the sections and definitions that matter, then one drafter per rule starts work, six at a time.

Each drafter reads sections, searches the contract, resolves defined terms, and must validate every edit anchor verbatim before it can submit. An independent verifier — a fresh context that never sees the drafter's reasoning — checks each proposal, and findings land in the workspace as they pass.

Nothing is written until counsel decides. J and K move, A accepts, E edits, R rejects. Here the cap that was limited to a single transaction becomes a mutual twelve-month cap with a floor; the licence is extended to affiliates; a missing convenience-termination right is inserted.
Accepted wording becomes memory. The next contract's liability cap starts from language this team has already approved — the same words every time.
Export writes a new copy of the file: real Word tracked changes, real margin comments citing the playbook rule, author Playbook Redliner — and every untouched paragraph verified byte-identical.
The assembler also drafts the issues memo: walk-away items first, then the fixes, then the clauses that were checked and left alone.

The hard case is a cap that reads twelve months' Fees, where Fees is defined two sections away as a one-off implementation fee. A frontier model with the whole contract in context resolves that in one prompt. What the pipeline adds is the edit: one validated redline that caps all charges with a floor — and it leaves the two decoy clauses alone.

On the pre-registered metrics the gap is no longer inside the noise. Complete redlines — every element of the position met, applied to the document, minimal — rise from {{B1_CRR}} to {{V3_CRR}}. On six forty-thousand-word contracts, F one goes from {{B1_LONG_F1}} to {{V3_LONG_F1}}, and applied tracked changes from {{B1_YIELD}} to {{V3_YIELD}}. And nothing is silently applied: unsure findings are escalated to a person.

Detection saturated on short contracts, so we pre-registered what the product is actually for — a complete redline, and the long documents counsel really receives — before running the final pipeline on them. The baseline stayed the same one prompt with the whole contract.

Round one taught us where the value was not: the document model bought anchoring, not F one; per-rule workers bought recall; the verifier bought validity; memory was an honest non-result; the monolith was removed. And round one's final pipeline did not beat the baseline on long documents at all — we report that. What moved the numbers was writing every playbook position as an explicit checklist, a drafter that must account for each element, a verifier that checks them one by one, and whole-document search planning for long contracts.
Give a specialist agent one rule and it will find a violation — the biggest quality jump in this project came from writing the semantics into the playbook, not from any model, tool or extra agent.
Playbook Redliner. Every number, every trajectory, and every tracked change reproduces from the repository with one command.
